title: I changed to a terrain/heightmap/ based system for my RTS game
author: Crignog
selftext:
I posted the other day about wasting time, and the bottom line was that it absolutely is still fun, so I'm just going to continue. One of the comments mentioned how flat the terrain was, which was something that had been on my mind a lot. I got Claude to create a short "trailer" to show case it a bit. I also recorded a bit of gameplay of me starting a match here [https://streamable.com/akzqqa](https://streamable.com/akzqqa) but it's very rough, almost all 3D models aren't in yet, UI is a bit jank etc. 

  
If anyone has any feedback, thoughts or ideas or want to see more of anything in particular I'd love to hear it :)

replies.author: Crignog
replies.body:
3D models are just going to be for resources/buildings/objectives. All units will stay as sprites :) Yeah UI is something I've struggled with massively, I used SpriteCook to generate some UI a while ago and just haven't updated it. No idea on the best route to making UI at the moment; any suggestions?

With regards to the blurring it's essentially creating two bands of blur that intensify the deeper into the band objects are. So a band at the top and bottom of the cameras view, with a 100% clarity band in the middle

replies.author: Polaricano
replies.body: Ah, I don't have a good suggestion for that specifically, but what works for me is going to websites like https://interfaceingame.com/ (I think https://www.gameuidatabase.com/ might also be good) and screenshot ting examples that I like.  I then prompt for designs in Figma and keep adjusting from there.

replies.author: Crignog
replies.body: Oh man thanks for those resources, that's great! How are you transferring designs from figma into your game engine?

replies.author: Upbeat-Strain-7999
replies.body: For Godot specifically, the simplest workflow is exporting your Figma panels as PNGs (or SVGs if you want them scalable) and building the UI with TextureRect, NinePatchRect, and containers in the editor. If you want to stay closer to the Figma layout, there are plugins like FigmaToGodot that import nodes directly, though they can be finicky. Honestly for an RTS, hand-placing panels in Godot after using Figma as a visual reference tends to give you more control than auto-import.

replies.author: Crignog
replies.body: Appreciate that a lot thank you! I will definitely be spending some time working on this :)

replies.author: Polaricano
replies.body:
https://preview.redd.it/qvpdn89vi0rh1.png?width=3412&format=png&auto=webp&s=47ea7ec01d49ba2e1b727d25fffb9b318c3c743f

This is a rough example, but you can take something like the BotW shop UI and convert it to another purpose, in my case I wanted a crafting menu.  I'm experimenting now with notifications/popups.  Animations can be handled in figma as well.

Once I have a design in figma Astra usually does a good job creating it in Unity. The figma MCP can be wonky (sometimes its unaware of what files or pages actually exist) so I paste the link to specific designs in the prompt.

replies.author: YYY003003
replies.body:
Hmm, thats a heavy question. I have always loved these kinds of sprites ever since I played fire emblem 23 years ago.

I am even slowly working on something vaguely like this, armies of sprites fighting in a traditional top down pixel map, with my unique twist on it. Since ive started I've realized the single most important thing whether people will give a first look at your game is if it is "aesthethic" to them.

So I think the effect youve created, "simple" as it is, its quite striking and inspiring. I love the way the grass feels on them, the trees feel a little blocky compared to the ground but Im not skilled enough to tell you how to fix that.

replies.author: Crignog

Also yes, the trees were replaced with these low poly ones for now as the generated ones were massive on triangles and bad for performance hahaha, I will probably swap these ones out soon!
